reference_reasoning.proposition: The dense basal planar defects are LPSO nanoplates, i.e. aggregates of four-layer Zn/Y-segregated fcc-type stacking faults rather than conventional stacking faults [n8]
reference_reasoning.assumption: The bright, heavy-atom-rich HAADF-STEM contrast specifically reflects Zn/Y segregation into a four-layer fcc-type stacking arrangement rather than being an artifact of thickness, tilt, or an unrelated heavy element, and the reversible density/thickness changes on heat treatment reflect the same defect population rather than a different phase appearing and disappearing [writer inference]
reference_reasoning.open: The exact atomic stacking sequence and segregation pattern within each four-layer block is not resolved beyond the 1 nm inset, and whether the density/thickness trend would continue or saturate with additional heat-treatment cycles beyond the three conditions tested is not addressed [writer inference]
reference_reasoning.handoff: Heat treatment sets nanoplate density and thickness: 9.8 per um and ~28 nm as-grown, ~0.3 per um and ~84 nm after 520 C, and ~9.0 per um and ~14 nm after the further 400 C anneal [n9]

dependency.why: The five TEM/STEM panels (F1b-F1f) directly and completely support both the phase identification (n8) and the density/thickness quantification (n9) without requiring any conclusion carried in from an earlier step

observations: Panel F8a shows that compressing along [11-20] at RT gives a yield stress of 167 MPa as-grown, which drops to 113 MPa after the 520 C anneal and recovers to 160 MPa after the further 400 C anneal [obs1].

Panel F2a shows that RT yield stress varies sharply by orientation: about 9 MPa for [1 1 -2 1.85], 148-165 MPa for [11-20], 143 MPa for [01-10], and [0001] does not yield but fractures at about 355 MPa [obs2].

Panel F2a also shows that between RT and 400 C the alloy's [11-20]/[01-10] yield stress falls only from about 165 to 105 MPa, while the gray pure-Mg reference falls much further, from about 270 to 15 MPa, and sits near 10 MPa in the soft orientations [obs3].
reference_reasoning.proposition: Yield stress is strongly orientation dependent, reaching about 145-165 MPa at RT in [11-20] and [01-10], roughly 11 times the yield stress of pure-Mg single crystal [n12].
reference_reasoning.assumption: The step assumes that the yield stresses measured on these crystals are attributable to the LPSO nanoplate microstructure identified and sized in step 1, rather than to some unrelated compositional or testing artifact [writer inference].
reference_reasoning.open: It remains open exactly how the specific nanoplate density and thickness values from step 1 map quantitatively onto the observed changes in yield stress across the as-grown, 520 C, and 400 C conditions [writer inference].
reference_reasoning.handoff: The next step carries forward that yield stress is strongly orientation dependent, reaching about 145-165 MPa at RT in [11-20]/[01-10], about 11 times that of pure-Mg single crystal [n12].

dependency.why: The question explicitly frames the mechanical evidence as building on the phase identity and nanoplate density/thickness measured in step 1, so interpreting the orientation-dependent and heat-treatment-dependent yield stress changes as effects of that microstructure requires the prior identification.

reasoning: Bright-field TEM with g=0002 reveals strong planar fault-like contrast lying on (0001), at a density of roughly ten plates per um [obs1].
HAADF-STEM shows these plates as bright, heavy-atom-rich bands only a few atomic layers wide, with a 1 nm inset resolving one such bright band [obs2].

Together the fault-like diffraction contrast and the heavy-atom-rich atomic-scale banding identify the dense basal planar defects as LPSO nanoplates, i.e. aggregates of four-layer Zn/Y-segregated fcc-type stacking faults rather than conventional stacking faults [n8].
TEM after annealing shows the 520 C/water-quenched specimen retains only one thick dark plate, while the further 400 C anneal restores many thin plates [obs3].

Quantifying this reversal, nanoplate count falls from 9.8 to 0.3 and back up to 9.0 per um while mean thickness rises from 28 to 84 and falls back to 14 nm across as-grown / 520 C / 520->400 C [obs4].

These paired counts and thicknesses establish that heat treatment sets nanoplate density and thickness: 9.8 per um and ~28 nm as-grown, ~0.3 per um and ~84 nm after 520 C, ~9.0 per um and ~14 nm after the further 400 C anneal [n9].

Taking the LPSO nanoplate phase and its density/thickness values as given, the [11-20] RT yield stress is 167 MPa as-grown, falls to 113 MPa after the 520 C anneal (when the nanoplates coarsen to ~84 nm and thin to ~0.3 per um), and recovers to 160 MPa after the further 400 C anneal restores the fine, dense nanoplates [obs1 step2].
This tracking of yield stress with the nanoplate density/thickness cycle in the same orientation supports treating the nanoplates as the strengthening feature [writer inference].

RT yield stress otherwise varies strongly with crystal orientation: ~9 MPa for [1 1 -2 1.85], ~148-165 MPa for [11-20], ~143 MPa for [01-10], while [0001] fractures at ~355 MPa without yielding [obs2 step2].

Between RT and 400 C the alloy's [11-20]/[01-10] yield stress falls only from ~165 to ~105 MPa, whereas the pure-Mg reference falls from ~270 to ~15 MPa and sits near 10 MPa in the soft orientations [obs3 step2].
Together these establish that yield stress is strongly orientation dependent and, in [11-20] and [01-10], reaches ~145-165 MPa at RT, about 11x the pure-Mg single crystal [n12].

Taking this ~145-165 MPa hard-orientation yield stress as given, a tensile [0001] test at RT shows flow stress starting at ~72 MPa, serrated between ~52 and ~80 MPa, with the specimen reaching ~45% plastic strain before fracture [obs1 step3].
The tensile gauge is filled with fine bands inclined to the [0001] tensile direction, across which the marked basal-plane trace kinks [obs2 step3].
These observations establish that in tension along [0001] the crystal elongates ~45% at 65-80 MPa by kink-band formation, the first bulk demonstration of tensile ductility by kinking [n18].
end_to_end.why_weakest: Step 3 carries forward the ~145-165 MPa hard-orientation yield stress from step 2, but the service-performance evidence is about the soft [0001] orientation yielding at only 65-80 MPa via kinking, so the numerical and orientation link between the two steps is only nominal rather than a direct continuation.
